title: Google Cloud europe-west4-a: Grid Transient, DRUPS Failure and Chiller Shutdown
operator: Google Cloud (data center provider not named)

severity.usersAffected: 24 VMware Engine private clouds of 20 customers, 9 Bare Metal Solution customers, and NetApp Volumes customers on all 6 clusters in europe-west4-a.
severity.tier: Single data hall: power loss to one row and hall-wide thermal shutdown

brief: On 15 July 2026 a 3 ms grid transient tripped both utility feeds at the facility hosting Google Cloud zone europe-west4-a. The side A rotary UPS failed, one row lost power on transfer, and the chiller controller dropped out so the pumps stopped while the backup cooling was out for construction. The hall reached 44°C and equipment was shut down; customer disruption lasted 14 hours 55 minutes.

magnitude.note: One data hall serving three specialised products; 33 named customers plus NetApp Volumes users. Duration (6): 14 h 55 min, inside the 12–24 h band. No cost is disclosed, so financial is judged moderate.

sequenceOfEvents.event: An electrical fault occurred on the utility grid upstream of the data center: a 3 ms voltage transient hits both utility feeds A and B, both utility breakers trip and the site transfers to its diesel rotary UPS (DRUPS).
sequenceOfEvents.source: Google Cloud incident report 3BvH3LVGcupoYqV6F4Nw: 'a 3ms voltage drop in the power feed'

sequenceOfEvents.event: Side B transfers to DRUPS without interruption. The DRUPS for side A fails to take over the load because of electrical component failures.
sequenceOfEvents.source: Google Cloud incident report 3BvH3LVGcupoYqV6F4Nw: 'failed to take over the facility load due to electrical component failures'

sequenceOfEvents.event: The chiller controller drops offline during the transient, so the chilled-water distribution pumps stop and cannot restart and chiller system A shuts down. The redundant cooling source is out of service because of known ongoing construction work.
sequenceOfEvents.source: Google Cloud incident report 3BvH3LVGcupoYqV6F4Nw: 'known ongoing construction work at the facility'

sequenceOfEvents.event: Google engineers were alerted to the infrastructure power loss by automated monitoring; the VMware Engine power-monitoring alert fires.

sequenceOfEvents.source: Google Cloud incident report 3BvH3LVGcupoYqV6F4Nw, NetApp timeline

sequenceOfEvents.event: The three rows on feed A transfer to feed B. Rows 1 and 2 transfer; Row 3 fails to transfer because an overload protection breaker trips, and loses both feeds.
sequenceOfEvents.source: Google Cloud incident report 3BvH3LVGcupoYqV6F4Nw: 'Row 3 failed to transfer to power feed B and lost power'

rootCause:
TRIGGER: a 3 ms voltage transient on the utility grid upstream of the data center hosting europe-west4-a tripped the utility breakers on both feeds A and B at 16:24 PDT on 15 July 2026, and the site transferred to its diesel rotary UPS (DRUPS).

POWER CHAIN: side B went to DRUPS cleanly. The side A DRUPS failed to take over the facility load due to electrical component failures, so the three rows on feed A had to transfer automatically to feed B. Two rows did. Row 3 hit an overload protection breaker trip and lost both feeds; Google attributes this to a load deployment discrepancy, still under investigation at the time of the report.

COOLING CHAIN: the same transient knocked the chiller controller offline. The chillers kept power but the chilled-water distribution pumps stopped and could not restart, so with no water flow chiller system A shut down. The redundant cooling source was unavailable because of known ongoing construction work at the facility. The hall reached 44°C two hours later and the equipment had to be shut down.

LATENT ROOT: three independent weaknesses lined up on one transient: a DRUPS that could not carry its load, a row whose load did not fit the surviving feed, and a cooling plant whose controls had no ride-through and whose redundancy had been removed for construction. The facility team's own fix, a portable UPS for the chiller controllers, indicates the controllers were not on protected power (analyst inference from the action taken).
contributingFactors: The side A DRUPS failed to take the load because of electrical component failures (Google report).
Row 3 tripped an overload protection breaker on transfer to feed B: a load deployment discrepancy, still under investigation (Google report).
The chiller controller dropped offline on the transient and the distribution pumps did not restart on their own (Google report).
The redundant cooling source was out of service because of known ongoing construction work (Google report).
Chiller controllers apparently lacked protected power: the fix was an interim portable UPS for them (analyst inference from the action).
Console servers needed an onsite technician to recover, which delayed network restoration after cooling returned (Google report, GCVE timeline).
Thermal shutdown was a manual procedure; Google is now automating shutdown for fast-moving thermal events (Google report).

lessonsLearnt: A cooling plant's controls are part of the critical load. If a 3 ms transient can drop the chiller controller, the cooling plant has no ride-through no matter how much the chillers can do.
Pumps that need a restart command after a power event are a single point of failure; restart-on-power-return or hand-mode fallback must be designed in and drilled.
Taking cooling redundancy out for construction turns the next routine event into a thermal emergency. Plan compensating measures for the construction window.
Automatic transfer schemes only work if each row's load fits the surviving feed. Track deployed load per row against single-feed capacity.
Thermal events move fast: 44°C two hours after the trigger. Shutdown triggers and onsite staffing must be faster than the temperature rise.
Recovery depends on out-of-band access: needing a technician on site for console servers lengthened the outage after cooling returned.
improvements: Safety and cooling: keep chiller controllers on protected power (interim portable UPS done) and review pump control redundancy (Google committed).
Design: investigate the DRUPS transfer failure and restore full A-side redundancy (swing DRUPS in place; investigation committed).
Design: resolve the Row 3 overload so every row fits one surviving feed (Google committed).
Monitoring: earlier alerts for power events and cooling excursions (Google committed).
Process: automated shutdown for fast thermal runaway, updated incident classification for staffing, joint runbooks and a monthly emergency drill with the data center team (Google committed).
Analyst recommendation (not in the report): treat removal of cooling redundancy for construction as a change that needs a compensating plan, such as temporary chillers or reduced load.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: One transient, three failures
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: A 3 ms dip should be a non-event for a site with two feeds, a rotary UPS on each side and redundant cooling. Here it found a failed DRUPS on side A, an overloaded row that could not move to side B, and a chiller controller with no ride-through while the second cooling source was out for construction. Each weakness alone would have been survivable.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cooling failed through its controls
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The chillers kept power. What stopped was the controller and therefore the pumps. The repair was to put the pumps in hand mode. Controls and pumps belong in the same protected-power and restart design as the chillers, or cooling capacity on paper is not capacity in an event.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Construction as a hidden degradation
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The redundant cooling source was out for known construction work. Planned degradation is common, but the record shows no compensating measure for the window, and the event happened inside it.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Speed of a thermal event
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: From transient to 44°C took about two hours; NetApp clusters shut themselves down after about an hour. Google ran manual shutdown procedures and is now automating them, and is changing incident classification so enough people are available during major data center events.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: What the record does not say
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The report does not name the data center provider, the DRUPS make or the failed components, the chiller or pump models, or the cost. It also does not say whether the committed actions due in August to October 2026 have been completed.

technicalDeepDive:
A rotary UPS bridges the gap to diesel with a flywheel; if its electrical components fail, the side it protects drops to the automatic transfer scheme. That scheme only works if every row's load fits the surviving feed: Row 3 tripped its overload protection, the textbook symptom of a row loaded beyond what one feed can carry alone (Google calls it a load deployment discrepancy).

The cooling failure is a controls failure, not a chiller failure. A brief transient reset or dropped the chiller controller; the pumps needed a restart command that never came. The quick fix was mechanical: pumps put in hand mode. With the redundant source out for construction there was no second loop, so the hall rose to 44°C in about two hours and Google shut down reachable equipment. Recovery then needed an onsite technician for console servers, which added time after cooling was back at 21:05.

fmea.scope: The power chain (utility feeds, rotary UPS on each side, row transfer between feeds) and the cooling chain (chiller controller, chilled-water pumps, redundant source) of the facility hosting europe-west4-a, plus Google's thermal shutdown and recovery. Analysed from Google's own reports; the facility provider is not named and its view is not on record.

modes.failureMode: The DRUPS fails to take over the side A load because of electrical component failures
modes.effect: Side A is lost; three rows must transfer to feed B, and one of them fails
modes.cause: Electrical component failures in the side A DRUPS; details not disclosed
modes.prevention: A rotary UPS on each side; automatic row transfer to the other feed
modes.detection: None recorded before the event; the failure showed only when the DRUPS was called on

rationale.S: It removes one whole power side; with the transfer scheme working it would have been survivable, so 8 rather than 9.
rationale.O: A rotary UPS failing at the moment of demand is uncommon but plausible: 'infrequent'.
rationale.D: No recorded test or alarm found the faulty components beforehand.

rationale.O: Rows drifting past single-feed capacity is a known operational risk: 'infrequent'.
rationale.D: Nothing caught the discrepancy before the transfer was demanded.

modes.function: Keep chilled water flowing to the data hall through a power disturbance
modes.failureMode: The chiller controller drops offline on the transient; pumps stop and do not restart, and chiller A shuts down
modes.effect: No chilled water to the hall; temperature reaches 44°C and equipment is shut down
modes.cause: Controller without ride-through on the transient; pumps depend on a restart command
modes.prevention: Chillers on power; redundant cooling source (unavailable at the time)
modes.detection: Remote monitoring alerted on high temperature at 16:32 and switch temperature alerts at 17:05

rationale.S: It forced a hall-wide thermal shutdown of every product in the zone's affected hall: 9. Not 10, because no hazard to people is recorded.
rationale.O: Controller dropouts on transients happen but are not frequent: 'infrequent'.
rationale.D: Temperature alerts came within minutes, but they did not stop the rise.

evidence.quote: the chilled-water distribution pumps stop and cannot restart

Restart workloads only after the hall is back inside the allowable range

modes.function: Provide a second source of cooling if the primary plant stops
modes.failureMode: The redundant source is out of service for known construction work when the primary plant stops

modes.cause: Planned degradation of cooling redundancy without a compensating measure in the record
modes.prevention: N+1 or 2N cooling design (degraded for construction)
modes.detection: Known to the facility; nothing recorded flagged the risk of running degraded

rationale.S: It removes the fallback that would have prevented the thermal event; scored 8 so the thermal outage is not counted at full weight twice.
rationale.O: Construction and maintenance windows recur through a facility's life: 'occasional'.
rationale.D: The degradation was known, but no recorded control weighed the exposure it created.
